I have farmed this land in Quzhou my whole life. I know the North China Plain rhythm — winter wheat goes in after the autumn harvest, summer maize follows after the wheat comes off. That rotation is what my father did, and what I have refined over sixty years. The land here is flat, the water table has been dropping steadily, and my joints remind me every morning that I cannot work the way I did at forty. But I still have 12 mu under my management, and I intend to make them productive.

For wheat, I will plant a proven improved variety — something like Jimai 22 or Shimai 15, which handles our dry springs well and resists lodging. I have learned from the researchers who come through Quzhou that splitting nitrogen — base application plus topdress at jointing — gives better uptake and saves money. I will irrigate three times: once before winter freeze sets in, once at jointing, once at grain filling. No more, because the aquifer cannot support it and the cost of water has risen. I use rotary tillage after maize harvest to incorporate stubble.

For summer maize, I direct-seed Xianyu 335 hybrid into the wheat stubble — no deep tillage needed, saves fuel and my back. Rainfall in July and August usually covers most water needs; I will irrigate once at silking if it is a dry year, maybe twice. I keep pesticide use minimal — one herbicide pass early, one spray for corn borer if scouting shows it warranted. My experience says two applications is enough to protect yield without wasting money.
